motivation: In 2007 Lorimer, McLaughlin, Bailes and colleagues found a single, millisecond-duration, highly dispersed radio burst in archival Parkes pulsar-survey data. Its dispersion measure implied an extragalactic origin. The discovery revealed an entirely new class of astrophysical phenomenon. Fast radio bursts are now known to occur thousands of times per day across the sky. Follow-up work has localized them to host galaxies at cosmological distances, linked at least some to magnetars, and used them as unique probes of the ionized baryons between galaxies, resolving the 'missing baryon' problem and constraining intergalactic magnetic fields. The finding came from careful, sensitive searches of pulsar data, and it opened a new domain of the transient radio sky. It has driven new instruments such as CHIME, ASKAP and MeerKAT, and a global research field. It shows how precision radio techniques can uncover new physics in extreme environments.
